```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: true
source(here::here("R", "setup.R"))
walk <- load_walk()
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Simulated data"}
All examples use simulated data from fictional studies. Results illustrate methods; they are not empirical findings.
:::

This answer key gives complete, executed solutions to the Module 5 workbook, with model answers to the written questions and marking notes.

```{r}
#| label: helpers
sched <- c(0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12)
f_mean <- sbp ~ visit_f * arm
cells  <- expand.grid(visit_f = levels(walk$visit_f), arm = levels(walk$arm))
cell_w <- function(a, v) as.numeric(cells$arm == a & cells$visit_f == v)
chg12  <- function(a) cell_w(a, "12") - cell_w(a, "0")
L_dic  <- list("SP - UC" = chg12("SP") - chg12("UC"),
               "EP - UC" = chg12("EP") - chg12("UC"))
```

## Guided exercises

### Exercise 1. Residual correlation structures (LO 5.1, 5.3)

```{r}
#| label: ex1a
walk$res_ols <- residuals(lm(f_mean, data = walk))
obs_cor <- walk |>
  select(id, visit_f, res_ols) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit_f, values_from = res_ols) |>
  select(-id) |>
  cov(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  cov2cor()
round(obs_cor, 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex1b
m_cs  <- gls(f_mean, data = walk, correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))
m_ar1 <- gls(f_mean, data = walk, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ visit | id))
m_exp <- gls(f_mean, data = walk,
             correlation = corExp(form = ~ month | id, nugget = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#| label: ex1c
rho_cs  <- coef(m_cs$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
phi_ar1 <- coef(m_ar1$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
p_exp   <- coef(m_exp$modelStruct$corStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
r012 <- c(CS  = unname(rho_cs),
          AR1 = unname(phi_ar1^5),
          EXP = (1 - p_exp[["nugget"]]) * exp(-12 / p_exp[["range"]]),
          observed = obs_cor["0", "12"])
round(r012, 3)
```

**Model answers.**

(i) The observed correlation between baseline and month 12 is `r round(r012["observed"], 2)`. The exponential model with nugget gives `r round(r012["EXP"], 2)`, closest to the observed value; compound symmetry gives `r round(r012["CS"], 2)`, too high because it ignores the decline with lag; AR(1) gives `r round(r012["AR1"], 2)` ($`r round(phi_ar1, 2)`^5$), much too low because its correlations decay geometrically towards zero.

(ii) AR(1) is defined on the integer positions of the measurements. `visit` (1 to 6) gives those positions and keeps them correct when a visit is missed; `month` is continuous and irregular. For actual times, use `corExp()` or `corCAR1()`.

(iii) The range is `r round(p_exp[["range"]], 1)` months. Without a random intercept, the single exponential has to reproduce both the stable person-level component (correlations that stay near 0.7 over a year) and the short-term serial component. It can only do this by decaying very slowly; the nugget (`r round(p_exp[["nugget"]], 2)`) takes care of the measurement error.

*Marking notes.* Accept AR(1) correlations computed for visit 1 to 6 as five steps. A common error is to use `phi^12`, treating months as steps; give partial credit if the reasoning about geometric decay is correct. Another is computing `obs_cor` on raw `sbp` rather than residuals; the values are then somewhat higher.

### Exercise 2. The marginal covariance of a random intercept and slope model (LO 5.3)

```{r}
#| label: ex2a
m_prim <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id), data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
G  <- as.matrix(VarCorr(m_prim)$id)
s2 <- sigma(m_prim)^2
Z  <- cbind(1, sched)
V  <- Z %*% G %*% t(Z) + diag(s2, length(sched))
dimnames(V) <- list(sched, sched)
round(V, 1)
round(cov2cor(V), 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex2b
all.equal(V, implied_cov_lmer(m_prim, sched), check.attributes = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex2c
var12 <- G[1, 1] + 2 * G[1, 2] * 12 + G[2, 2] * 12^2 + s2
c(by_hand = var12, from_V = V["12", "12"])
```

**Model answers.**

(i) The implied variance is `r round(V["0","0"], 1)` mmHg² at baseline and `r round(V["12","12"], 1)` at month 12. Because $\operatorname{Var}(y_{it}) = \tau_0^2 + 2\tau_{01}t + \tau_1^2t^2 + \sigma^2$ with a negative covariance $\tau_{01} = `r round(G[1,2], 2)`$, the variance first falls slightly (minimum near $t = -\tau_{01}/\tau_1^2 = `r round(-G[1,2] / G[2,2], 1)`$ months) and then rises as the $\tau_1^2t^2$ term grows.

(ii) The implied correlation between months 0 and 1 is `r round(cov2cor(V)["0","1"], 2)`, below the observed `r round(obs_cor["0","1"], 2)`. The model has no serial correlation, so it cannot make measurements one month apart more alike than the random intercept and slope allow. It misses the short-term serial correlation.

*Marking notes.* The most common error is forgetting `diag(s2, 6)` (giving $ZGZ^\top$ only), or using `VarCorr()` standard deviations instead of variances.

### Exercise 3. Heterogeneous variances and REML comparisons (LO 5.2, 5.4)

```{r}
#| label: ex3a
m_exp_het <- update(m_exp, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit_f))
het_r <- coef(m_exp_het$modelStruct$varStruct, unconstrained = FALSE, allCoef = TRUE)
round(het_r, 3)
a_het <- anova(m_exp, m_exp_het)
a_het
```

```{r}
#| label: ex3b
m_exp_lin <- gls(sbp ~ month * arm, data = walk,
                 correlation = corExp(form = ~ month | id, nugget = TRUE))
anova(m_exp_lin, m_exp)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex3c
a_ml <- anova(update(m_exp_lin, method = "ML"), update(m_exp, method = "ML"))
a_ml
```

**Model answers.**

(i) No. The SD ratios range from `r sprintf("%.3f", min(het_r))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(het_r))` and the LRT on REML fits (same mean model) gives $\chi^2_5 = `r round(a_het$L.Ratio[2], 2)`$, `r fmt_p(a_het[["p-value"]][2])`.

(ii) nlme warns that the fitted objects have different fixed effects and that REML comparisons are not meaningful. REML maximises the likelihood of error contrasts that depend on $X$, so REML likelihoods for different mean models are not comparable.

(iii) Only the ML comparison is valid. It gives $\chi^2_{`r a_ml$df[2] - a_ml$df[1]`} = `r round(a_ml$L.Ratio[2], 1)`$, `r fmt_p(a_ml[["p-value"]][2])`: the categorical-time mean model fits much better than linear time, because the true trajectories level off after about six months.

*Marking notes.* Accept "the REML comparison is not valid" without the error-contrast explanation for partial credit. Students who report the REML LRT in (b) as evidence should lose the marks for (iii).

### Exercise 4. A boundary test for the clinic variance (LO 5.5)

```{r}
#| label: ex4
m_clinic <- lmer(sbp ~ visit_f * arm + (1 + month | id) + (1 | clinic),
                 data = walk, control = lmer_ctrl)
lt <- lr_test(m_prim, m_clinic)
lt$p_mixture <- p_boundary_mixture(lt$chisq)
lt
```

**Model answers.**

(i) The null value (variance 0) lies on the boundary of the parameter space. Under the null, the estimated variance is zero about half the time, and the LR statistic is then exactly zero, so its null distribution is a 50:50 mixture of a point mass at zero and $\chi^2_1$ [@self1987]. Comparing with $\chi^2_1$ alone overstates the p-value. Here the naive p-value is `r formatC(lt$p, format = "f", digits = 4)` and the mixture p-value `r formatC(lt$p_mixture, format = "f", digits = 4)`, exactly half.

(ii) Statistically, the clinic variance is clearly non-zero (LR = `r round(lt$chisq, 1)`, estimated clinic SD `r round(attr(VarCorr(m_clinic)$clinic, "stddev"), 1)` mmHg). By design, participants were recruited and randomised within clinics, so clinic is a natural grouping factor (a stratification factor should usually be reflected in the analysis). A good answer also notes that the treatment estimates barely change, so including or excluding it is not critical for the estimand, and that this should be prespecified.

### Exercise 5. A singular fit in a small sample (LO 5.5)

```{r}
#| label: ex5a
set.seed(8)
small <- filter(walk, id %in% sample(unique(walk$id), 30))
m_small <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id), data = small, control = lmer_ctrl)
VarCorr(m_small)
isSingular(m_small)
```

Trying several seeds shows that most samples of 30 give a regular fit:

```{r}
#| label: ex5-seeds
sing <- sapply(1:20, function(s) {
  set.seed(s)
  d <- filter(walk, id %in% sample(unique(walk$id), 30))
  isSingular(suppressMessages(lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month | id), data = d,
                                   control = lmer_ctrl)))
})
mean(sing)
```

```{r}
#| label: ex5b
m_small_unc <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 + month || id), data = small, control = lmer_ctrl)
m_small_ri  <- lmer(sbp ~ month * arm + (1 | id), data = small, control = lmer_ctrl)
small_cmp <- bind_rows(lapply(list(correlated = m_small, uncorrelated = m_small_unc,
                                   intercept_only = m_small_ri), function(m) {
  s <- coef(summary(m))["month:armEP", ]
  data.frame(estimate = s[["Estimate"]], se = s[["Std. Error"]], singular = isSingular(m))
}), .id = "random_effects")
small_cmp
```

**Model answers.**

(i) With seed 8 the correlation between random intercept and slope is estimated at `r round(attr(VarCorr(m_small)$id, "correlation")[1,2], 2)`, a boundary value; the 2 × 2 covariance matrix has rank one. In `r round(100 * mean(sing))`% of 20 seeds the fit was singular.

(ii) No. The slope SD in the full data is clearly positive (true value 0.35 mmHg/month); with 30 participants there is too little information to estimate the covariance matrix, and boundary estimates are common even when the true parameters are interior.

(iii) The estimate of `month:armEP` hardly changes between specifications (`r paste(round(small_cmp$estimate, 2), collapse = ", ")`), and the standard errors are similar. In this sample the uncorrelated model is `r if (isSingular(m_small_unc)) "also singular (the slope variance is estimated as zero), so the intercept-only model is the only non-singular option" else "not singular"`. Reasonable answers: report the simpler non-singular model (uncorrelated or intercept-only, whichever is not singular) and state that the full model was singular; or keep the prespecified model and report that the conclusions do not change. Either is acceptable if justified and transparent.

## Independent exercises

### Exercise 6. Choose and defend a covariance model (LO 5.1, 5.4, 5.6)

```{r}
#| label: ex6
w4 <- filter(walk, clinic %in% 1:4)
c(participants = n_distinct(w4$id), observations = nrow(w4))
w4$res_ols <- residuals(lm(f_mean, data = w4))
obs_cor4 <- w4 |> select(id, visit_f, res_ols) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = visit_f, values_from = res_ols) |> select(-id) |>
  cov(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  cov2cor()

mods4 <- list(
  "Compound symmetry"   = gls(f_mean, data = w4, correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id)),
  "Exponential + nugget" = gls(f_mean, data = w4,
                               correlation = corExp(form = ~ month | id, nugget = TRUE)),
  "Unstructured"        = gls(f_mean, data = w4, correlation = corSymm(form = ~ visit | id),
                              weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | visit_f)),
  "Random intercept + slope" = lme(f_mean, random = ~ 1 + month | id, data = w4),
  "Random intercept + exponential" = lme(f_mean, random = ~ 1 | id, data = w4,
                               correlation = corExp(form = ~ month | id, nugget = TRUE)))
cmp4 <- data.frame(model = names(mods4),
                   n_cov = sapply(mods4, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")) - 18,
                   AIC = sapply(mods4, AIC), BIC = sapply(mods4, BIC), row.names = NULL) |>
  mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC), dBIC = BIC - min(BIC))
knitr::kable(cmp4, digits = 1)
```

The heatmap uses the implied-covariance function from the notes.

```{r}
#| label: ex6-heat
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Clinics 1 to 4: observed residual correlations and those implied by two candidate models."
implied_cov <- function(model, times = sched) {
  k <- length(times); C <- diag(k)
  cs <- model$modelStruct$corStruct
  if (!is.null(cs)) {
    if (inherits(cs, "corCompSymm")) {
      C <- matrix(coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE), k, k); diag(C) <- 1
    } else if (inherits(cs, c("corAR1", "corARMA"))) {
      C <- coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE)^abs(outer(1:k, 1:k, "-"))
    } else if (inherits(cs, "corExp")) {
      p <- coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE)
      nug <- if ("nugget" %in% names(p)) p[["nugget"]] else 0
      C <- (1 - nug) * exp(-abs(outer(times, times, "-")) / p[["range"]]); diag(C) <- 1
    } else if (inherits(cs, "corSymm")) {
      C[lower.tri(C)] <- coef(cs, unconstrained = FALSE); C <- C + t(C) - diag(k)
    }
  }
  vs <- model$modelStruct$varStruct
  s <- if (is.null(vs)) rep(1, k) else
    coef(vs, unconstrained = FALSE, allCoef = TRUE)[as.character(times)]
  V <- model$sigma^2 * diag(s) %*% C %*% diag(s)
  if (inherits(model, "lme")) {
    G <- as.matrix(getVarCov(model)); Z <- cbind(1, times)[, seq_len(ncol(G)), drop = FALSE]
    V <- Z %*% G %*% t(Z) + V
  }
  dimnames(V) <- list(times, times); V
}
mat_long <- function(M, label) {
  data.frame(row = factor(rep(rownames(M), ncol(M)), levels = rownames(M)),
             col = factor(rep(colnames(M), each = nrow(M)), levels = colnames(M)),
             value = as.vector(M), model = label)
}
bind_rows(mat_long(obs_cor4, "Observed"),
          mat_long(cov2cor(implied_cov(mods4[["Compound symmetry"]])), "Compound symmetry"),
          mat_long(cov2cor(implied_cov(mods4[["Random intercept + exponential"]])),
                   "Random intercept + exponential")) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = unique(model))) |>
  ggplot(aes(col, row, fill = value)) + geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", value)), size = 2.4) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F7FBFF", high = "#2171B5", limits = c(0.3, 1),
                      name = "Correlation") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) + facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled month", y = "Scheduled month") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: ex6-values
#| include: false
best4_aic <- cmp4$model[which.min(cmp4$AIC)]
best4_bic <- cmp4$model[which.min(cmp4$BIC)]
```

**Model answer.** In clinics 1 to 4 (`r n_distinct(w4$id)` participants) the lowest AIC belongs to the `r best4_aic` model and the lowest BIC to the `r best4_bic` model. A justification might read: "The covariance model must describe a stable between-participant component and correlation that declines with time between visits, and must handle irregular visit times. A random intercept with exponential serial correlation in actual time and a nugget does all three with four covariance parameters. `r if (best4_aic == "Random intercept + exponential" && best4_bic == best4_aic) "It had the lowest AIC and BIC of the candidates" else "Its information criteria were close to the best of the candidates"`, its implied correlations match the observed pattern, and it is far more parsimonious than the unstructured covariance, which would be fragile with about 45 participants per arm at month 12. A random intercept and slope model will be reported as a sensitivity analysis."

*Marking notes.* Award marks for: same mean model in all fits; REML used; a table with AIC and BIC; a heatmap; a justification that refers both to the statistics and to substantive features (irregular times, parsimony, sample size). Do not require a particular final choice; with a smaller sample, BIC may favour simpler structures than in the full data. Penalise choosing the unstructured model only "because it has the highest log-likelihood".

### Exercise 7. Does the covariance model change the answer? (LO 5.6)

```{r}
#| label: ex7
eff4 <- bind_rows(lapply(names(mods4), function(nm) {
  m <- mods4[[nm]]
  e <- if (inherits(m, "gls")) emmeans(m, ~ visit_f * arm, mode = "df.error") else
    emmeans(m, ~ visit_f * arm)
  s <- summary(contrast(e, L_dic["EP - UC"]), infer = TRUE)
  data.frame(model = nm, estimate = s$estimate, se = s$SE,
             lower = s$lower.CL, upper = s$upper.CL)
}))
knitr::kable(eff4, digits = 2)
```

**Model answer.** Across the five models the EP versus UC difference in mean change ranges from `r round(min(eff4$estimate), 2)` to `r round(max(eff4$estimate), 2)` mmHg, and the standard error from `r round(min(eff4$se), 2)` to `r round(max(eff4$se), 2)`. The point estimate depends little on the covariance model. Compound symmetry gives the smallest standard error (`r round(eff4$se[eff4$model == "Compound symmetry"], 2)`), which is likely too small because it assumes that baseline and month 12 are as highly correlated as adjacent visits. The conclusion (a clear reduction in the enhanced programme relative to usual care) is the same under every model.

### Exercise 8. Variance by arm (LO 5.2, 5.4)

```{r}
#| label: ex8
m_riexp     <- lme(f_mean, random = ~ 1 | id, data = walk,
                   correlation = corExp(form = ~ month | id, nugget = TRUE))
m_riexp_arm <- update(m_riexp, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | arm))
arm_r <- coef(m_riexp_arm$modelStruct$varStruct, unconstrained = FALSE, allCoef = TRUE)
round(arm_r, 3)
a_arm <- anova(m_riexp, m_riexp_arm)
a_arm
```

**Model answer.** The residual SD ratios relative to usual care are `r paste(names(arm_r), sprintf("%.3f", arm_r), collapse = ", ")`. The LRT on REML fits (same fixed effects, two extra parameters, both interior under the null, so the usual $\chi^2_2$ applies) gives $\chi^2 = `r round(a_arm$L.Ratio[2], 2)`$, `r fmt_p(a_arm[["p-value"]][2])`. `r if (a_arm[["p-value"]][2] < 0.05) "There is evidence that the residual variance differs between arms." else "There is no evidence that the residual variance differs between arms, consistent with the simulation, in which every arm has the same variance components."` Note that `varIdent` here scales only the residual part ($R_i$); the random-intercept variance is common to all arms.

*Marking notes.* A variance ratio is not on the boundary when testing equality (ratio = 1), so no mixture is needed; students who apply the mixture should lose a mark.

### Exercise 9. Write the methods paragraph (LO 5.6)

**Model answer.** "The primary analysis used a linear mixed model with a separate mean for each arm at each scheduled visit (visit by arm interaction) and a random intercept and random slope on actual time since randomisation for each participant, with an unstructured 2 × 2 covariance matrix, fitted by REML. This covariance model was prespecified because it describes stable between-participant differences and individual trends and accommodates irregular visit times. Its adequacy was checked by comparing implied and observed correlations between visits and by the semivariogram of normalized residuals. Sensitivity analyses used an unstructured residual covariance and a random intercept with exponential serial correlation in continuous time and a nugget; the estimated differences in mean change at month 12 differed from the primary analysis by less than 0.1 mmHg."

*Marking notes.* Look for: the mean model, the random-effects structure, the estimation method, the reason for the choice (prespecification and substantive features), how adequacy was checked, and sensitivity analyses. Numbers should match the notes.
